Toxic trace elements have aroused the interest of the scientific community and the organizations responsible for food safety in recent decades. Numerous reviews have been made of aspects related to the presence of these elements in food, and committees of experts such as the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) or the FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA) have published monographs in which toxicological reference values have been modified on the basis of new information. The aim of this review is to summarize the most important existing information on the processes that these contaminants may undergo during their transit through the gastrointestinal tract, and the toxic effect that this transit may have on the gastrointestinal epithelium. It must be borne in mind that the gastrointestinal epithelium is the first barrier that these elements encounter when they are ingested, and it limits their absorption ratio and subsequent entry into the systemic circulation. Moreover, the digestive tract cannot be considered to be a mere onlooker; a series of processes may take place in it which alter the form that the toxic element originally has in the food. The presence of food components and endogenous substances, the gastrointestinal epithelium, and the microbial flora are key factors not only in the process of digestion and absorption but also in processes of transformation that can produce important changes in the chemical form of these elements. The chemical changes are ultimately translated into modifications of the absorption and toxicity of these contaminants.

## 1.2. Dietary sources for cadmium

As already mentioned, exposure to toxic trace elements is mainly due to ingestion of food and in some cases to consumption of water with high levels of the contaminant. This section provides a summary of existing information about toxic trace element contents and indicates the main dietary sources which contain them.

## 1.1. Dietary sources for lead

Lead (Pb) is mainly present in inorganic form in food products, although in recent decades, as a result of advances in analytical chemistry, organic forms have also been identified. Some wines from southern France show concentrations of trimethyl lead in a range of 8.1e112 ng/L (Lobinski et al., 1993). Chen et al. (2014) also found trimethyl lead chloride in oyster samples (0.23 mg Pb/kg dry weight, dw). Furthermore, Pb can coordinate with sulfhydryl or amino groups of various proteins or peptides in the food matrix (Srinivas et al., 2007).

EFSA examined 94,126 analytical data for Pb in food, collected during a nine-year period (EFSA, 2010); the highest amount of Pb was found in game meat (mean: 3.1 mg/kg), followed by edible offal from game animals (mean: 1.25 mg/kg) and alga-based supplements (mean: 1.02 mg/kg). The latest report on cadmium (Cd) produced by the European Food Safety Authority's panel on contaminants (EFSA, 2009a) shows that the main dietary sources of this element are cereals and cereal products, vegetables, nuts and pulses, starchy roots or potatoes, and meat and meat products. However, the highest concentrations are found in seaweed, seafood, chocolate, fungi, oilseeds and edible offal.

The existing studies on seaweed indicate that the highest Cd concentrations occur in certain species: Porphyra spp., Undaria pinnatifida and Hizikia fusiforme (Almela et al., 2006; Dawczynski et al., 2007). In seafood products, the highest values are found in shellfish, especially in bivalve mollusks (Amiard et al., 2008; Bendell, 2009), which sometimes exceed the limit established by the Commission Regulation (EU) N488/2014 (1 mg/kg). Mushrooms also have concentrations that exceed the legal values. Kala[] c and Svoboda (2000) report that the content in Boletus aestivalis, Leccinum scabrum, Calocybe gambosa, Armillaria mellea and Russula cyanoxantha growing in unpolluted areas can be up to 5 mg/kg dw; and that in species of the Agaricus genus the concentration can be as much as 50 mg/kg dw. Bearing in mind the maximum Cd concentration permitted by the European Union regulation in cultivated mushrooms other than Agaricus bisporus, Pleurotus ostreatus

and Lentinula edodes [1.0 mg/kg fresh weight (fw), equivalent to 10 mg/kg dw], mushrooms of the Agaricus genus could present a food safety problem. Among foods of plant origin, products derived from cocoa have some of the highest Cd concentrations. Mounicou et al. (2003) report high concentrations in cocoa powder obtained from processing of cocoa beans (0.09e1.8 mg/kg). In a study on chocolate from Brazil, Villa et al. (2014) show that dark chocolate has higher concentrations of Cd than milk and white chocolate, and this concentration is directly proportional to the quantity of cocoa in the formulation.

EFSA's CONTAM panel (EFSA, 2009a) has established a tolerable weekly intake (TWI) of 2.5 mg/kg bw. In the same report, EFSA indicates that part of the European population has a Cd intake close to or even exceeding the TWI, and therefore a substantial reduction in dietary exposure to this metal is recommended (EFSA, 2009a). Weekly dietary intake estimates in the United States are in the range of 1.9e3.0 mg/kg bw for non-vegetarians. Vegetarians and regular consumers of bivalve mollusks and wild mushrooms are estimated to have, respectively, weekly dietary Cd exposures of 5.4 mg/kg bw, 4.6 mg/kg bw and 4.3 mg/kg bw (IARC, 2012).

## 1.3. Dietary sources for mercury

Mercury (Hg) can be found in food in divalent inorganic form [Hg(II)] or as methylmercury (CH3Hg). Fish considered as marine predators (swordfish, shark, bonito, and tuna) are the types of food that usually have the highest Hg content, mainly in the form of CH3Hg (Storelli et al., 2002, 2003; Sahuquillo et al., 2007). The Hg concentrations reported in swordfish (0.031e4.9 mg/kg), tuna (0.60e1.47 mg/kg), and shark (0.22e2.5 mg/kg) (Monteiro and Lopes, 1990; Branco et al., 2007; Torres-Escribano et al., 2011) are sometimes higher than the limits established by the legislation for seafood products of this kind (1 mg/kg). Processed seafood products derived from large predators generally have lower Hg concentrations (<1 mg/kg) (Burger and Gochfeld, 2004; Yang et al., 2015).

In products of plant origin, Hg concentrations are far lower and mainly correspond to inorganic Hg (Cappon, 1981; Jedrzejczak, 2002), except for mushrooms, in which high concentrations have been found in some species. A study conducted in Poland shows that mushrooms are capable of accumulating Hg from the soil, with bioconcentration factors ranging between 2 and 210 (Falandysz et al., 2014). In Europe there is no legislation on this aspect; however, China limits the Hg concentration to 0.1 mg/kg fw, which is approximately equivalent to 1 mg/kg dw. In the Southern part of Spain mushrooms of the Boletus aereus species have been found with high Hg concentrations (10.28 ± 2.92 mg/kg dw) (Ostos et al., 2015). Kala[] c and Svoboda (2000) also report high values (>1 mg/kg) in samples of the Boletus, Agaricus, Lepista and Macrolepiota genera, with especially noteworthy concentrations in Lepista nuda and Agaricus arvensis which can reach 20 mg/kg dw.

The World Health Organization has established a provisional tolerable daily intake (PTWI) of 3 mg/kg bw for inorganic Hg (JECFA, 2011) and of 1.6 mg/kg bw for CH3Hg (JECFA, 2003). Countries such as the United Kingdom, Canada and Spain have provided recommendations to limit the consumption of fresh and frozen tuna, swordfish, and shark by sensitive populations (FSA, 2003; Health Canada, 2008; AECOSAN, 2011). In the year 2012, EFSA warned that the 95th percentile dietary exposure in the European population was close to or above the PTWI for all age groups, and high fish consumers may exceed the PTWI by up to approximately six-fold (EFSA, 2012b). This can be seen in countries with a high consumption of seafood products such as Japan, where intakes ranging between 0.38 and 6.79 mg/ kg bw/week have been found (Iwasaki et al., 2003).

## 1.4. Dietary sources for arsenic

Arsenic (As) can be found in food in inorganic form [arsenate, As(V), and arsenite, As(III)] or in a series of organic forms. Among the forms found in food so far, inorganic species, particularly As(III), are the most toxic. Total As contents are particularly noteworthy in seafood products, but the As species that predominate are considered innocuous. In most fish, arsenobetaine is the main species, while in some types of mollusks, mainly bivalves, remarkable concentrations of arsenosugars are described. The concentrations of inorganic As do not usually exceed 0.3 mg/kg (Munoz[~] et al., 2000); however, high values have been reported in mussels from very specific areas (Sloth and Julshamn, 2008). Among foods of marine origin, the contents found in algae are notable. H. fusiforme is the edible seaweed in which the highest total As concentrations have been systematically detected, sometimes exceeding 100 mg/kg (Almela et al., 2002), making it a highrisk food.

In foods of terrestrial origin, notable concentrations are found in mushrooms and rice. Edible mushrooms have As concentrations much higher than those found in other vegetables (0.1e147 mg/kg dw, Vetter, 2004). Rice has been studied in more detail because it is a staple food. Contents in rice are higher than in other cereals, with concentrations of 0.25 mg/kg or more being commonly detected (Zavala and Duxbury, 2008). It has been shown that rice contains As(III), As(V), and dimethylarsinic acid [DMA(V)], while monomethylarsonic acid [MMA(V)] has been detected in a small number of samples. Inorganic As represents variable percentages of total As in rice (27e93%) (Torres-Escribano et al., 2008).

The World Health Organization established the maximum tolerable level of total As in drinking water as 10 mg/L, which has been adopted by most countries. However, there are no maximum limits for inorganic As in food in most countries. Only China, Australia, New Zealand and European Union regulate the level of inorganic in some food products. Additionally, recommended intake values have been established. In a review of the latest scientific evidence, JECFA (2011) determined the lower limit of the benchmark dose for a 0.5% increased incidence of lung cancer from epidemiological data to be 3 mg/kg bw per day (2e7 mg/ kg bw per day based on the range of estimated total dietary exposure).

In some Asian and Latin American countries, where concentrations of inorganic As in water exceed the recommended maximum values, water and food cooked with this contaminated water are the main sources of inorganic As exposure. The intake values in these countries are higher than the established reference values. In countries where there is no As contamination, food is the main source of inorganic As. In a recent document from EFSA (2009b) it was shown that, in Europe, inorganic As exposure from food and water ranges from 0.13 to 0.56 mg/kg bw/day, with cereals, bottled water, coffee, beer, rice, fish, and vegetables being the main contributors. Yost et al. (1998) reported daily dietary intakes of inorganic As ranging from 8.3 to 14 mg/day in the United States and from 4.8 to 12.7 mg/day in Canada for various age groups. Inorganic As intake by the Japanese population is higher (mean: 24 mg/day); with cereals and algae constituting 90% of the total inorganic As intake in adults (Oguri et al., 2014).

## 2. Transformation during transit through the gastrointestinal (GI) tract

In the digestive tract, trace elements that are bound to the food matrix undergo a series of processes that permit their release. In solution, these elements may then undergo redox reactions,

methylation or demethylation, or binding to molecules or macromolecules. These transformations are due to the presence of food components and digestive enzymes in the lumen and to the presystemic metabolism resulting from the action of the microbiota and the epithelial cells of the GI mucosa. Most of the studies on transformations refer to the action of the microorganisms present in the large intestine. The other components have not been well characterized as catalysts of changes in the chemical forms of trace elements.

The components of the food matrix that are released during digestion of food may have a reduction potential (vitamin C, vitamin E and carotenoids), a considerable oxidative capacity (lipid peroxides resulting from processing or storage of fat-rich foods), or a high affinity for metal ions (amino acids, peptides, proteins). There are few studies on these aspects and they focus mainly on As. For example, in a study using a static GI digestion model, Calatayud et al. (2013) showed changes in the oxidation state of arsenic species initially present in vegetables. In vegetables cooked with As(V), MMA(V) and DMA(V), after digestion it was found that a considerable percentage of the pentavalent forms of arsenic had been reduced [0.1e22% As(III), 4e35% MMA(III) (monomethylarsonous acid) and 5e26% DMA(III) (dimethylarsinous acid)]. According to those authors, the changes were the result of the As species coming into contact with reducing substances from the vegetables assayed (garlic, broccoli and asparagus). Zhao et al. (2014) also conclude that the GI digestion process may reduce As(V) in seaweed. They suggest that the cause of this transformation may be the acid phase in the stomach.

In addition to food components, the enzymes and compounds naturally present in the lumen or induced by the process of digestion may interact with toxic trace elements. It has been seen that after ingestion of soil contaminated with Pb there is a process of complexation in the lumen as a result of which Pb3(PO4)2 and Pbbile complexes are the main forms (Oomen et al., 2003). The formation of complexes with bile salts has also been reported for Cd. These complexes are more stable than those resulting from complexation with Pb (Feroci et al., 1995).

Metabolism by the epithelial cells of the intestine may also bring about important changes in the forms of As that subsequently enter the systemic circulation. A recent study shows that the Caco-2 cell line, a model of the intestinal epithelium, is capable of metabolizing As(III) to mono- and dimethylated species in trivalent and pentavalent state (Calatayud et al., 2012a). This is a first indication which shows that the epithelium does not act merely as a physiological barrier. It is also considered that the Cd that enters the intestinal epithelium induces production of metallothioneins, lowmolecular-weight metal-binding proteins rich in cysteine residues, to which it may bind. The data concerning the effect of this binding on Cd absorption is contradictory. For some authors this binding implies a smaller absorption (Min et al., 1991), but other studies have shown that metallothioneins do not affect Cd absorption (Flaig et al., 2003).

The microflora present in the large intestine is a decisive factor in the presystemic transformations of toxic trace elements (DiazBone and Van de Wiele, 2010). Studies using samples of feces from 14 human volunteers and isolated gut segments of mice incubated under anaerobic conditions show the formation of volatile derivatives of Pb and As (Michalke et al., 2008). Meyer et al. (2008) conducted a study to identify the microorganisms in the human intestine that are responsible for the volatilization of metals and metalloids, in which Hg and As were evaluated. The study analyzed the transforming capacity of methanoarchaeal human gut inhabitants and strains of the main bacterial phyla (members of Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, Actinobacteria and Bacteroidetes). The authors did not find evidence for volatilization of Hg, and only the

methanoarchaeal strains were capable of generating volatile methylated species [CH3AsH2, (CH3)2AsH, (CH3)3As] from inorganic As (KH2AsO4). Although recent studies have not shown volatilization of Hg, Rowland et al. (1978) demonstrated that the contents of the cecum and small intestine of the rat metabolized CH3HgCl to a volatile product over a period of 3e4 days, and they confirmed that this volatilization was due to microflora, especially those of the cecum. With regard to Cd, no studies have been conducted to evaluate the formation of volatile species by the intestinal flora.

Microbial transformations of toxic trace elements do not only generate volatile species; the formation of other kind of species has also been documented, especially for Hg and As. In the case of Hg, various studies have shown that animals without intestinal microbiota have a lower intestinal excretion of Hg after oral exposure to CH3Hg (Seko et al., 1981; Rowland et al., 1984). This reduction in excretion has been related to a decrease in demethylation of the organic form to inorganic Hg by the intestinal flora. This demethylation was previously verified by Rowland et al. (1977) using contents of the rat cecum. They demonstrated synthesis of HgCl2 from CH3Hg in vitro under aerobic and anaerobic conditions. They also showed that this synthesis was inhibited by antibiotics and by filtration of the cecal contents through membrane filters. The opposite process has also been observed in isolates of intestinal flora; for example, a study by Ludwicki (1990) showed that two reactions took place in incubation of the intestinal contents of rats with HgCl2 (2.5e12 mg/mL): a minority methylation to CH3Hg and demethylation to Hg[0] .

Regarding As, it has been shown that the contents of the intestinal cecum of rats and mice, or the flora isolated from those portions of the intestine, play an important part in its presystemic metabolism. Hall et al. (1997) showed that, in anaerobic conditions, a large proportion (up to 40%) of the inorganic forms of As [As(III) and As(V)] was transformed into mono- and dimethylated species after 21 h of incubation, with the monomethylated form predominating. The transformation was inhibited when the concentration of inorganic As increased, and was faster for As(III), indicating that the reaction of reduction of As(V) to As(III) was a limiting step. Kuroda et al. (2004) showed that Escherichia coli A3-6 isolated from rat cecum transformed DMA(V) into metabolites with a higher degree of toxicity in the presence of cysteine, but they did not identify the compounds. Subsequently, Kubachka et al. (2009) identified those metabolites as three thiolated species: dimethylthioarsinic acid [DMTA(V)], dimethyldithioarsinic acid [DMDTA(V)] and trimethylarsine sulfide (TMAS), with DMDTA(V) predominating.

These transformations observed in intestinal contents of rodents have subsequently been confirmed in in vitro assays using feces isolated from humans. Alava et al. (2013) conducted a study on biotransformation with aqueous standards of As(V) and rice in which As(V) and DMA(V) were the predominant forms. In those assays the As species were incubated with a cultured suspension sampled from the colon compartment of the Simulator of the Human Intestinal Microbial Ecosystem (SHIME) previously inoculated with a pooled fecal sample from volunteers. In both cases, formation of DMA(III), MMA(III) and monomethylmonothioarsonic acid [MMMTA(V)] occurred as minor metabolites.

The possible transformation of more complex organic arsenic species with a lesser degree of toxicity has also been evaluated in order to verify whether their toxicity can increase after ingestion as a result of microbial action. Harrington et al. (2008) showed that aerobic enteric flora isolated from healthy humans could degrade arsenobetaine to metabolites of greater toxicity [DMA(V), dimethylarsinoylacetic acid (DMAA) and trimethylarsine oxide (TMAO)]. Transformations of arsenosugars to thiolated analogs have also been demonstrated (Conklin et al., 2006), using mice cecal

## 3. Bioavailability and intestinal transport mechanisms of Pb, Cd, Hg and As

Bioavailability (the fraction of a compound that reaches the systemic circulation after intestinal absorption) and the mechanisms involved can be evaluated by means of in vivo, in situ or in vitro assays. For in vivo studies there are two possible approaches: evaluation of the appearance of the compound in plasma at different times or quantification of the compound in excreta. With in situ models using perfusion techniques in which the animals are anesthetized it is possible to achieve greater control of certain parameters. Although the animals undergo a surgical process, their neural, endocrine, lymphatic, and mesenteric blood supplies remain intact, and therefore all the transport mechanisms present in a live animal should be functional (Griffin and O'Driscoll, 2008). In the case of in vitro approaches it is possible to work with brush border membrane vesicles or everted intestinal ring or sacs of various portions of the gastrointestinal tract of laboratory animals and with cell lines derived from colorectal cancers (Caco-2, HT-29).

## 3.1. Lead

A study of gastrointestinal absorption of lead chloride carried out in humans showed a mean absorption of 21.3% of the dose, with a range from 10.4 to 47.7%. Male subjects had a lower mean absorption of 18.1% of the dose, compared with a mean of 26.9% in females (Moore et al., 1979). There appears to be some increase in uptake as the period of fasting is extended (58.6e66.7%; Heard and Chamberlain, 1982). Absorption in adult rats can also be considered moderate (89-day-old rats: 16.0 ± 3.4%), but is much higher in young rats (16-day-old rats: 83.3 ± 3.3%) (Forbes and Reina, 1972).

The studies just cited were conducted using aqueous standards of Pb salts, but there are also studies that evaluate absorption using food with Pb. In general, Pb uptake in adults is markedly lower with consumption of meals than under fasting conditions (Rabinowitz et al., 1980). Yannai and Sachs (1993) found great variability when they studied absorption of Pb from various kinds of diet in rats (corn-silage meal: 48 ± 19%, corn: 59 ± 8%, commercial fish meal: 26 ± 9%, fish meal from polluted areas: 82 ± 8%). Hallen and[] Oskarsson (1995) evaluated bioavailability of Pb from various milks in 14-day-old suckling rats and showed that 6 h after administration there was absorption of 50% from water and human milk, 45% from infant formula and cow milk, and 36% from rat milk. Hunt et al. (2009) made an estimate of bioavailability of Pb in pigs after administration of hunter-killed venison meat and showed that the peak of Pb concentration in the blood of those pigs (mean: 2.29 mg/ dL) was greater than in blood of control pigs who had been given venison without ammunition fragments (mean: 0.63 mg/dL). In humans, an association has also been demonstrated between consumption of game meat and levels of Pb in blood (Tsuji et al., 2008; Iqbal et al., 2009); however, this correlation has not been shown in all studies (Haldimann et al., 2002).

According to data in the literature, Pb intestinal transport includes both a carrier-mediated component and passive diffusion. Diffusion of Pb through the intestinal membrane has been noted in various in vitro studies (Blair et al., 1979; Aungst and Fung, 1981), in which the rate of transport into the serosal compartment and the tissue uptake increased linearly with increasing concentration of Pb cation under certain conditions. It has also been shown that there is saturable transport, which seems to be predominant, and some studies have even demonstrated the participation of transporters in

the transport of Pb. The transporters that have been studied most are those related to the transport of elements such as Fe and Zn, because absorption of Pb decreases in their presence (see section 4.1). For example, Bannon et al. (2002) demonstrated that divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1), the main transporter of non-heme Fe in enterocytes, expressed in yeast mutants facilitated transport of Pb, and that overexpression of DMT1 in HEK293 cells also increased uptake of Pb. These results suggest that DMT1 is a transporter for Pb. However, in a later study using Caco-2 as a model of the intestinal epithelium the same authors did not find participation of DMT1 in Pb uptake (Bannon et al., 2003). Another transporter that has been noted is the Zrt/Irt-related protein 14 zinc transporter (ZIP14). In studies made after cloning of this transporter in oocytes of Xenopus laevis, Nebert et al. (2012) suggest the participation of this transporter in intestinal uptake of Pb, given that the presence of Pb reduces the entry of Zn. However, inhibition of the transporter due to the toxic nature of Pb, rather than competition between these two elements, cannot be ruled out.

## 3.2. Cadmium

It has been estimated that in humans there is low intestinal absorption (1e7%) after oral administration of inorganic Cd (Shaikh and Smith, 1980). Studies in experimental animals (mice, rats, and monkeys) have shown that 0.5e8% of Cd(NO3)2 or CdCl2 is absorbed after a single oral exposure (JECFA, 2001). The bioavailability of Cd from food or in the presence of food is similar to that observed in aqueous solutions. For example, Flanagan et al. (1978) administered a breakfast spiked with CdCl2 to 21 healthy young adults and obtained an absorption not exceeding 7.5%. Vahter et al. (1996) also observed very low absorption of Cd in non-smoking women after ingestion of shellfish diets (median Cd intake: 22.3 mg/day). These absorption ratios may increase in certain conditions, especially in connection with nutritional deficits. It has been seen that mineral nutrient status could be an important factor that controls the extent of oral Cd absorption and tissue accumulation (see section 4.2). It has also been shown that there is greater absorption of the inorganic forms of Cd than of Cd bound to metallothioneins (Sugawara and Sugawara, 1991) or phytochelatins (Fujita et al., 1993).

The mechanisms of transport across the intestinal epithelium are not fully characterized. Intestinal absorption of Cd is characterized by high accumulation within the intestinal mucosa and a low rate of transfer into the organism (Elsenhans et al., 1997). In a study using Caco-2 cells as a model, Jumarie et al. (1999) concluded that Cd transport occurs exclusively by a transcellular route and that saturation of the intracellular high-capacity binding sites is the rate-limiting step in Cd absorption. On the other hand, Schümann et al. (1990) showed that a certain tissue accumulation is required in order to obtain a transfer of Cd, and that increasing tissue accumulation precedes an increase in transfer rates.

It has been seen that there are certain interactions between essential metals and Cd at the site of intestinal absorption, which point to some common features in the absorption pathways (Elsenhans et al., 1997). In fact, several studies have observed that DMT1 is involved in transport of Cd in the intestine (Park et al., 2002; Bannon et al., 2003). It has also been shown that the ZIP family of zinc transporters can play a part in transcellular transport of Cd (Himeno et al., 2009), and it has even been verified that knockdown cells for ZIP14, the major isoform in the intestine, have lower uptake of this metal (Fujishiro et al., 2012). In addition to carrier-mediated transport, some studies reveal the existence of passive diffusion (Endo, 2002; Lecoeur et al., 2002).

## 3.3. Mercury

Studies in animals and humans have shown that CH3Hg is absorbed more efficaciously than inorganic Hg. Sasser et al. (1978) observed that CH3Hg in ligated segments of rat intestines was absorbed 17e35 times faster than inorganic Hg salt. In squirrel monkeys (Berlin et al., 1975) and rats (Walsh, 1982) exposed to CH3Hg, 95% of an ingested dose was absorbed. Piotrowski et al. (1992) evaluated whole-body retention (content in internal organs, blood, muscles, bones, and skin) of HgCl2 4 h after dosing. In low and moderate doses (0.2e12.5 mg/kg) the retention was 3e4% of the dose. In high doses (17.5 and 20.0 mg/kg), the values were 8.7 and 6.5%. The studies just cited were conducted using aqueous solutions administered intragastrically.

There are very few studies on the absorption of Hg ingested with food and they show a similar tendency to the aqueous standards, greater absorption of the organic form. Endo et al. (2003) investigated absorption, distribution, and excretion of Hg in rats after a single oral dose of whale liver highly contaminated with Hg in inorganic form (1980 mg/kg). The results showed that about 95% of the dose of Hg was excreted in feces and less than 0.05% in urine. On the basis of this excretion, the authors estimated that the rate of absorption of Hg was about 5%. However, these data are not very precise as fecal excretion data tend to underestimate the absorption rate because they cannot distinguish unabsorbed Hg from recirculation of Hg into the intestine during the experimental period. Yannai and Sachs (1993) showed that absorption of Hg present in fish, mostly CH3Hg, is high (75e93%). In the same study, the absorption of inorganic Hg (48%) that they found after administration of corn contaminated with Hg during cultivation was not as low as that reported by other authors.

It has been suggested that intestinal absorption of Hg(II) in rats takes place in two steps. Initially the inorganic Hg is accumulated in the intestinal mucosa and subsequently it is internalized and reaches the systemic circulation (Piotrowski et al.,1992). Studies in situ on intestinal absorption of Hg(II) have shown that the transport changes with variation in pH and concentrations of Cl[] and Na[þ] , and in the presence of chelating substances and cysteine (Endo et al., 1988, 1991). In an in vitro study using Caco-2 cell line, V[] azquez et al. (2015a) demonstrated that paracellular diffusion and the passive transcellular pathway are not important in the transport of Hg(II). They also showed that transcellular transport of Hg(II) has an active component, is dependent on pH and concentration of Na[þ] , and is inhibited in the presence of cationic and neutral amino acids and Mn(II). The same authors later demonstrated that transport of Hg(II) bound to cysteine can take place via the b[0,][þ] amino acid transporter (Vazquez et al., 2015b[] ) and that the passage of Hg(II) across the epithelial monolayer in saline form may be mediated by the transporter DMT1 (Vazquez[] et al., 2015c).

With regard to CH3Hg, Vazquez[] et al. (2014a) showed that the main pathway for the entry of CH3Hg in the form of CH3HgCl is by transcellular passive diffusion, which is in agreement with the lipophilic nature of this form of mercury. However, when it is bound to cysteine the participation of passive diffusion is not great. The same authors (V[] azquez et al., 2015b) also showed recently, in gene silencing studies, that the B[0,][þ] system participates in entry of CH3Hg bound to L-cysteine into the intestinal epithelium. Mori et al. (2012) also suggest participation of a member of the large neutral amino acid transporters (LAT) in uptake of CH3Hgecysteine by epithelial cells in the intestine.

## 3.4. Arsenic

Intestinal absorption of As depends on the chemical form in which it is present. In vitro studies on the apparent permeability

coefficient of the more toxic forms of As, using Caco-2 as a model of the intestinal epithelium, show the following order in magnitude of absorption: DMA(III) > MMA(III) >> As(III) >> As(V) > MMA(V) > DMA(V) (Calatayud et al., 2010, 2011). In general, the trivalent forms are absorbed more efficaciously than the pentavalent forms.

In humans, most of the studies on As bioavailability have concentrated on inorganic As, showing that absorption is high (Bettley and O'Shea, 1975; Pomroy et al., 1980). In experimental animals, the absolute bioavailability of a single dose of As(III) or As(V) administered by gavage is more than 75% (Freeman et al., 1995; Roberts et al., 2002; Juhasz et al., 2006). The absorption reported for DMA(V) is more variable, with bioavailability ranging between 80% in rodents (Vahter et al., 1984) and 33% in swine (Juhasz et al., 2006). A study using swine shows that absorption of MMA(V) (16.7 ± 5.0%) is less than that of the inorganic and dimethylated forms (Juhasz et al., 2006). Absorption of the more complex organic forms is also high. The few studies on this aspect, concentrating mainly on arsenobetaine and arsenocholine, indicate that they are almost totally absorbed in the GI tract of mice (Vahter et al., 1983; Marafante et al., 1984).

There are few in vivo studies on the bioavailability of As from food. Juhasz et al. (2006) showed different bioavailabilities for two types of rice [Quest (33.1 ± 3.2%) and Basmati (89.4 ± 9.4%)] and related this to the arsenical composition. In Quest rice the major As species is DMA(V), whereas in Basmati rice there is a predominance of the inorganic form, which has a greater degree of absorption. The same authors evaluated other foods of plant origin and observed bioavailabilities ranging between 98% in beans and 50% in lettuce (Juhasz et al., 2006).

Transport mechanisms at intestinal level have been studied recently. As(V), As(III), and MMA(III) showed mixed components of trans- and paracellular transport, while DMA(III) is mostly transported transcellularly, involving energy-dependent processes (Calatayud et al., 2010, 2011). Various studies have shown or suggested the participation of Na-dependent phosphate transporter (NaPi), aquaglyceroporins (AQP), glucose permeases (GLUT), and organic anion transporting polypeptides (OATP) in intracellular uptake of As(III) and/or As(V) (Lu et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2006; Villa Bellosta and Sorribas, 2008; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2014). Specifically, at intestinal level, Calatayud et al. (2012b) have demonstrated the participation of the isoforms OATPB, AQP10, and GLUT5 for As(III) and NaPiIIb for As(V) cellular uptake, using siRNAtransfected Caco-2 cells as a model.

## 4. Dietary factors that may affect absorption processes

Numerous studies have shown that absorption processes may be modulated by components of the diet. The process may be affected by the contaminant binding with compounds that reduce its solubility or its passage through the epithelium or by competition between the contaminant and the dietary components for the mechanisms of entry to the epithelium. This has been amply documented, especially for Pb and Cd, and some of these compounds have even been classified as dietary strategies to reduce the quantity of the contaminant that reaches the systemic circulation.

## 4.1. Lead

In vitro studies have shown that the presence of certain foods modifies the bioaccessibility (the soluble fraction of a compound obtained after GI digestion that is available for absorption) and the absorption of Pb. The leaf and stem of water spinach significantly reduce the bioaccessibility of Pb (25%) and its cellular uptake

(26e64%) (Yang et al., 2012). The addition of vinegar also significantly reduces the bioaccessibility of Pb in samples of oysters (Amiard et al., 2008).

Some of the food components that may reduce absorption of Pb have been identified, such as Ca, Fe, P, and Zn. Feeding mice with a Ca-deprived diet for 2 weeks prior to dosage stimulated the absorption of Pb from water by more than 100% (Van Barneveld and Van den Hamer, 1985). Bradman et al. (2001) compared blood Pb levels of Fe-deficient and Fe-replete children living in low, medium, or highly contaminated environments. Blood Pb levels were higher for Fe-deficient children for each tertile of exposure; the largest differences among groups were observed in children living in the most contaminated areas. In rats, as dietary Zn level rose from 8 to 200 mg/L, absorption and blood Pb levels reduced by about 60% (Cerklewski and Forbes, 1976). Mykkanen[€] et al. (1984) evaluated the effect of increased concentrations of K2HPO4 in the diet (0.6e2.2%) on Pb absorption from in situ ligated duodenal loops of prefasted chicks. The results showed a significant decrease in the intestinal retention and transfer of Pb to the systemic circulation in the two highest phosphate groups. The authors demonstrated that part of this effect was due to precipitation of Pb, possibly by formation of Pb3(PO4)2. Most of the studies on this aspect suggest that these elements reduce Pb absorption, but there are some articles that do not show clear effects (Rosado et al., 2006). In a study carried out to evaluate the effect of Zn and/or Fe supplementation on blood Pb levels of children attending schools in the neighborhood of a smelter complex, no difference was observed among the supplemented groups and the placebo group (Rosado et al., 2006).

The presence of phytates also brings about reductions in the bioavailability of Pb. In rats given a diet supplemented with phytate (10 g/kg) and Pb (200 mg/kg) for 4 weeks there was a reduced accumulation of Pb in bone and liver and a lower blood concentration. The reduction was greater in the presence of Ca (6 g/kg) (Rose and Quarterman, 1984). Bullock et al. (1995) characterized this reduction over a broad range of pHs (3e7) and at different phytate:Pb ratios and observed a minimum solubility of Pb at a metal ion:phytate ratio in the range 5:1e3:1 over the whole pH range. It is considered that the formation of phytate-Pb or Caphytate-Pb co-precipitates is the cause of the decrease in the solubility of Pb in the presence of this insoluble fiber.

As with minerals, a deficiency of protein in the diet also brings about greater absorption of Pb. A study carried out in rats using casein as dietary protein demonstrated that diets containing 10e15% protein had no effect on Pb absorption; however, diets containing 5% protein increased blood Pb concentration (Barltrop and Khoo, 1975). Vitamin C has an effect similar to that of dietary protein. The relationship between vitamin C status and Pb accumulation in the body was examined cross-sectionally among 747 e men aged 49 93 years. In multiple regression models adjusting for age, education level, smoking, and alcohol consumption, men with the lowest vitamin C intake (<109 mg/day) had a mean blood Pb level higher than men with the highest vitamin C consumption (>339 mg/day) (Cheng et al., 1998).

Some components that increase the entry of Pb into the bloodstream have also been described. In this regard, Mykkanen[€] and Wasserman (1982) showed that vitamin D3 did not significantly affect the accumulation of Pb by intestinal tissue but accelerated Pb movement across the basolateral membrane in in situ studies using chicks. Vitamin B1 has the same effect; its presence increases absorption of Pb, possibly by formation of a complex that is more soluble than inorganic Pb at intestinal pH (Reddy et al., 2010). Ingestion of fat also leads to an increase in absorption of Pb. Thus, Gallicchio et al. (2002) found statistically significant positive associations between blood Pb and total fat as well as saturated fat in children living in old, urban houses.

Some studies indicate that probiotics are good tools for reducing oral exposure to toxic trace elements. Studies with Pb show that the binding of various strains of lactic bacteria to this metal is fast (Halttunen et al., 2007a) and can endure in time (48 h), which makes these bacteria a suitable strategy for reducing intestinal absorption of this metal. The rapid uptake suggests that binding occurred passively to the surface of the bacteria rather than by accumulation inside the cell (Halttunen et al., 2007a). In the only in vivo study that has been conducted, Tian et al. (2012) showed that Lactobacillus plantarum CCFM8661 protects against Pb toxicity by decreasing Pb levels in the blood and tissues and by preventing oxidative stress. They found that this protective effect is due to this strain's ability to sequester Pb ions.

## 4.2. Cadmium

Absorption of Cd is affected by compounds and elements similar to those described for Pb. An effect of phytate has been seen in studies using everted sacs from small intestine of rats. The greatest decrease in Cd absorption due to phytic acid was observed at a Ca:phytic acid molar ratio of 5:1 (Turecki et al., 1995). Various studies have shown that the presence of wheat bran or whole wheat reduces absorption of Cd in rats (Moberg et al., 1987; Wing, 1993; House et al., 2003). Lind et al. (1998) demonstrated that GI absorption of Cd after exposure for 9 weeks to three fiber-rich foodstuffs (wheat bran, sugar-beet fiber, and carrots) was lower in the group receiving the wheat-bran diet. The authors concluded that this was due to the phytate content, which was higher in wheat bran. The effect of dietary fiber has also been shown in humans; in a study conducted in 57 non-smoking women, 20e50 years of age, the authors showed that the levels of Cd in blood were negatively correlated with consumption of fiber (Berglund et al., 1994).

There is evidence that marginal intakes of Zn, Fe, and Ca cause accumulation of Cd in the duodenum in rats, which results in a greater rate of Cd absorption and a greater accumulation in the internal organs (Reeves and Chaney, 2004). Gallagher et al. (2011) showed that for every mg/kg increase in body Fe, urine Cd decreased by 0.003 mg/g creatinine in 599 never-smoking women, e aged 20 49 years. The reduction in intestinal transport of Cd in the presence of minerals is believed to be due to competition for the same transport mechanisms (see section 3.2). Some studies also e suggest that Cd Zn interactions at the stage of their GI absorption are closely related to the affinity of both metals for intestinal metallothioneins (Brzoska and Moniuszko-Jakoniuk, 2001[] ), but the relevant data are contradictory.

Dietary protein also affects Cd bioavailability. In short-term studies, higher Cd levels were observed in the liver, kidney, and whole body of mice fed low-protein diets for 24 h before and after an oral dose of Cd. Conversely, in long-term studies, rats with highprotein diets were found to have significantly higher concentrations of Cd in the liver and kidney than rats that were fed the lowprotein diet (Revis and Osborne, 1984). These results suggest that the effect of dietary protein may be associated with the length of exposure.

The strategy of using probiotics has also succeeded in reducing the bioavailability of Cd. L. plantarum CCFM8610, a probiotic with good Cd-binding capacity, is able to protect mice from acute and chronic Cd toxicity via its intestinal sequestration (Zhai et al., 2014). The authors observed that oral administration of CCFM8610 significantly increased fecal Cd and reduced tissue accumulation of the element, also decreasing liver oxidative stress.

## 4.3. Mercury

Some studies evaluate the effect of certain foods on the

bioaccessibility of Hg. Extracts of green tea and black tea, even in small quantities, have a very significant effect on the bioaccessibility of Hg, with decreases ranging between 35% and 91% (Shim et al., 2009; He and Wang, 2011; Ouedraogo[] and Amyot, 2001). Instant coffee also produces a reduction ranging between 10% and 50% in the bioaccessibility of Hg in fish such as mackerel, tuna, and shark (Ouedraogo and Amyot, 2001[] ). Soy protein reduces the bioaccessibility of Hg (44e87%) from seafood products in a dose-dependent manner (Shim et al., 2009). A decrease in the bioaccessibility of Hg has also been observed in the presence of grapefruit juice (Shim et al., 2009; He and Wang, 2011). This indicates that some food components may affect solubilization of Hg present in foods during digestion and therefore may affect its subsequent absorption. There are numerous in vivo studies which show that some components of the diet can reduce the toxicity of orally administered Hg species; however, few studies analyze whether this beneficial effect may be due to modification of the bioavailability of Hg (Chapman and Chan, 2000).

A reduction in the effect of CH3Hg and an increase in its elimination have been shown in animals treated with various kinds of fiber (Rowland et al., 1986; Shim et al., 2009). It is known that CH3Hg undergoes extensive enterohepatic recirculation. Fiber has been shown in vitro to bind Hg, and as fiber is non-absorbable it is proposed that fiber in the diet interrupts enterohepatic recirculation by binding CH3Hg, thus leading to an increased rate of elimination. Moreover, as indicated in section 2 of this review, the intestinal microflora metabolize CH3Hg to inorganic Hg, favoring its excretion. As dietary fiber has profound effects on the metabolic activity of the gut flora, fiber may also influence CH3Hg reabsorption via an effect on bacterial Hg metabolism.

Other dietary components that have been proposed as possible protectors against the toxicity of Hg are probiotics (Brudnak, 2002). In fact, it has been shown that some lactic bacteria can bind Hg in divalent inorganic form (Kinoshita et al., 2013). In buffer solution, Hg(II) (1 mg/L) biosorption assay data showed that all the selected strains (50 Lactobacillus,19 unidentified lactic acid bacteria derived from yogurt, 8 Weissella, 4 strains of Pediococcus, 2 of Streptococcus, and 2 Enterococcus) reduced Hg(II) concentrations to under 0.15 mg/L. There are no in vivo studies that demonstrate the efficiency of lactic bacteria in reducing the intestinal absorption of Hg.

## 4.4. Arsenic

Studies by Kenyon et al. (1997) suggest that feeding a diet lower in fiber or “bulk” to female B6C3F1 mice decreased absorption of a single oral dose of As(V) (5 mg/kg) by ~10% compared to a standard diet. In a study with swine fed with vegetable products contaminated with As, Juhasz et al. (2008) showed that the bioavailability of this element is greater in rice than in lettuce, chard, and radish. They suggest that this may be because As bioavailability is influenced by the non-digestible polysaccharide component of the vegetable. Gonzalez[] et al. (1995), using two complementary approaches, an in vivo determination of GI absorption in rats and an in situ technique, showed that As(V) absorption decreased in the presence of phosphate. This effect was subsequently verified in vitro using Caco-2 cells and increasing concentrations of phosphate (Calatayud et al., 2010) and was related mainly to the fact that the two elements share transport mechanisms in the intestinal epithelium because of their structural similarity (Calatayud et al., 2012b). Fullmer and Wasserman (1985) showed that vitamin D3 administration to rachitic chicks was effective in significantly elevating duodenal As(V) absorption, acting primarily to enhance serosal transport.

With regard to the possible effect of probiotics, Singh and Sarma (2010) showed that Lactobacillus acidophilus is capable of

eliminating considerable proportions of As(III) in aqueous solution at pH 7 after 4 h of contact (30e60%). In most of the cases, it is necessary a modification of the bacteria surface in order to sequester the negatively charged arsenic species (Halttunen et al., 2007b).

## 5. Evaluation of toxic effects at gastrointestinal level

Acute exposure to high doses of toxic trace elements causes GI disturbances. Prolonged exposure to doses higher than those recommended also has negative effects on the digestive system, but there are fewer studies on this aspect than on what are considered as target organs.

## 5.1. Lead

Acute exposure to Pb causes GI disturbances in adults at blood concentrations of 100e200 mg/dL, although effects have been observed at concentrations as low as 40e60 mg/dL (ATSDR, 2007a).

Inorganic Pb compounds are classified as probably carcinogenic to humans (group 2A) by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC, 2006). Several studies have focused on cancer risks among workers exposed to inorganic Pb compounds and some of them have suggested that there may be risk of GI cancers among these workers (Fu and Boffetta, 1995; Gerhardsson et al., 1995). However, in most of the studies there are various uncertainties that cast doubt on the results (no direct exposure data, no inclusion of important confounders, low sample size, co-exposure with other possible carcinogens). Chronic exposure at work also causes nausea, vomiting, anorexia, constipation, and abdominal cramps (RAIS, 1994). However, there are no population studies aimed at determining the effects on the digestive system of prolonged exposure to Pb through the diet.

Studies in animals have shown effects on the digestive tract and its functions. Ryden and Walsh (1987) demonstrated that subchronic exposure to Pb (4% for 7 weeks) in rats slows gastric emptying. Vahedian et al. (2011) found that Pb exposure (1% for 3e4 weeks) affects gastric motility via the nitric oxide pathway. In a study on rodents chronically exposed (9 months) to low concentrations of Pb (0.1%), Kosik-Bogacka et al. (2011) showed a strong inhibitory effect of Pb on electrophysiological parameters, changes in intestinal permeability, disappearance of junctional occludin from localization at cellecell contacts and appearance within the basal portion of cytoplasm and within nuclei of enterocytes, and decreased amount of mucus. Changes were also observed in another important component for proper functioning of GI processes, the intestinal microflora. Sadykov et al. (2009) showed that 2 weeks of exposure produced dysbacteriosis, with a drastic increase of E. coli in comparison with other microbial groups. Breton et al. (2013) also showed a change in the composition of colon microbiota in mice exposed to PbCl2 (100e500 mg/kg) for 8 weeks.

It has also been demonstrated that Pb enhances damage produced at digestive level by other toxic substances. Olaleye et al. (2007) observed that oral Pb acetate exposure for 15 weeks (100 mg/L) increased the formation of gastric ulcers in animals treated with ethanol by interfering with oxidative metabolism.

## 5.2. Cadmium

In rats and mice, severe necrosis, hemorrhage, and ulcers in the GI epithelium were observed following acute-duration oral exposure to >30 mg/kg bw. In humans, the necropsy of a fatal case revealed hemorrhagic necrosis of the stomach, duodenum and jejunum (Buckler et al., 1986).

IARC has classified cadmium and cadmium compounds as

carcinogenic to humans (Group I, IARC, 1993). This classification is based on studies on individuals exposed through inhalation and is due to the appearance of lung cancer. However, despite the concern expressed by experts, there is no convincing evidence that cadmium compounds induce cancer following oral exposure, although there are some studies that indicate greater incidence of prostate, breast, and pancreas cancers (ATSDR, 2012). In no case has an increase in the prevalence of tumoral lesions at GI level been reported.

Prolonged exposure affects both the structure and the functionality of the GI epithelium. In rats subchronically exposed (30 days) to high doses of CdCl2 (15 mg/kg), a reduction was observed in gastric parietal cells, accompanied by a decrease in basal acid output (Asar et al., 2000). The authors observed important structural changes at cellular level (swollen canalicular profiles, brokendown tubulovesicles, and degenerated mitochondria). At intestinal level, effects on the structure of the colon have been reported. In mice dosed with CdCl2 (50 mg/kg), Singh et al. (2011) showed induction of histopathological damage evidenced by emptied goblet cells, lacerated and suppressed mucosa, destruction of surface epithelium, marked decline in mucin production, and hemorrhage. This epithelial destructuration may be the cause of the increase in permeability observed in animals (Kim et al., 2014) and in cell models of the intestinal epithelium (Duizer et al., 1999).

Some studies indicate that the effect of Cd on the intestinal immune system is responsible for the toxicity observed after exposure to this element. In a study conducted in mice (single dose, 25e100 mg/kg bw), Zhao et al. (2006) found an increase in expression of the proinflammatory cytokine MIP-2 (macrophage inflammatory protein-2) and in myeloperoxidase activity, and infiltration of inflammatory cells in the lamina propia. Kim et al. (2014) reported that subchronic exposure to Cd produces an effect on gut immune homeostasis and innate immunity. Mice exposed to Cd exhibit a significant reduction of secretory IgA and also are more responsive to oral administration of cholera toxin.

As in the case of Pb, exposure to Cd affects the intestinal microflora. In a study conducted by Fazeli et al. (2011) in rats e exposed to Cd through drinking water (23 50 mg/kg) for 45 days, the authors found dysbiosis which affected the small intestine more, suggesting site-specific toxicity. In general, they observed that Gram-negative bacteria were less sensitive to Cd than Grampositive bacteria. However, Breton et al. (2013) did not observe effects on viability of murine intestinal microbiota in prolonged exposure (CdCl2, 8 weeks, 20e100 mg/kg), although they did find changes in composition with lower genus diversity.

## 5.3. Mercury

The degree of toxicity of Hg and the places where it predominantly exerts its toxicity depend on the chemical form in which it is present. In acute exposure, Hg generally produces effects on the GI tract, like the other toxic trace elements. In prolonged exposure, the inorganic form has the greatest repercussion on the digestive tract, which is considered one of its target organs.

Acute ingestion of Hg(II) and CH3Hg is highly irritating to tissues of the GI tract. In humans there are reports of extensive precipitation of intestinal mucosal proteins, diarrhea, colicky abdominal pain, oropharyngeal pain, ulceration, and hemorrhages throughout the length of the GI tract after accidental ingestion of HgCl (ATSDR, 1999). The corrosive effect of CH3Hg is also reflected in the ulcerative esophagitis seen in cats dosed orally with 1.3 mg/kg bw/day and in the necrosis, edema, and congestion of the stomach in dogs dosed with 0.43 or 0.64 mg/kg bw/day and pigs given 0.64 or 0.86 mg/kg bw/day (JECFA, 2000).

Studies on prolonged exposure have reported inflammatory

processes and necrosis at gastric level in mice exposed to inorganic Hg (59 mg/bw/day, 5 days/week) for 2 weeks (NTP, 1993). In a chronic exposure study conducted in rats, 12e14% of the males exposed to 1.9 or 3.7 mg/bw/day presented inflammatory processes in the cecum and a significant increase in the incidence of hyperplasia in the stomach (NTP, 1993). Ulceration of the glandular stomach was observed in mice after 2 years of exposure to CH3HgCl (0.86 mg/kg/day) in the diet (Mitsumori et al., 1990). Chronicduration oral exposure to inorganic and organic Hg may, therefore, result in various GI symptoms in humans, with possible damage to intestinal tissues (ATSDR, 1999). However, epidemiological studies in populations continuously exposed through food do not focus their evaluation on effects at GI level.

In vitro studies support the effects observed in vivo and try to explain what causes them. Bohme[€] et al. (1992) showed that inorganic Hg and CH3Hg (5e50 mM) produced changes in permeability of the epithelium. Evaluation of the morphology of the epithelium revealed that, at least for inorganic Hg, this increase in permeability was due to loosening of tight junctions, alterations of enterocytes, and loss of continuity of the epithelium. The effect on intercellular junctions was also observed in a study on intestinal epithelial cells by Vazquez[] et al. (2014b), in which they showed redistribution of the cytoskeleton and zonula occludens 1 (ZO-1), a protein of intercellular junctions.

## 5.4. Arsenic

The toxicity of this element varies according to the chemical form in which it is present. The inorganic forms are the most toxic forms that have been found in food so far, and therefore they are the ones that have been studied in most detail. It must be borne in mind, however, that these inorganic forms give rise to mono- and dimethylated metabolites with a different degree of oxidation, and may be bound to sulfhydryl groups (Thomas et al., 2007), some of which are more toxic than the inorganic forms (Hughes et al., 2011).

Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain are very common symptoms in humans following oral exposure to inorganic arsenicals, both in acute high-dose exposure and after repeated exposure to lower doses; these effects are probably due to direct irritation of the GI mucosa (ATSDR, 2007b). Specific dose levels associated with the onset of these symptoms have not been identified. The cause of death in acute exposure to high doses is massive fluid loss due to secretion from the GI tract. On postmortem examination, esophagitis, gastritis, and hepatic steatosis are reported (Ratnaike, 2003).

With regard to chronic exposure to inorganic As, IARC has classified this species as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1, IARC, 2004). It is one of the few compounds that have been shown to cause cancer in humans through consumption of drinking water. Most epidemiological studies show greater prevalence of cancers of the skin, bladder, kidney, and lung (Smith et al., 1999). In a study carried out in Taiwan in a population exposed to high concentrations of As in drinking water (0.35e1.14 mg/L), Chen et al. (1985) also demonstrated a major prevalence of colon cancer [standardized mortality ratio, SMR: 117e203 (males); 126e210 (females)].

The GI symptoms in chronic exposure are similar to those observed in acute exposure. In populations chronically exposed to inorganic As through drinking water, symptoms of dyspepsia, gastroenteritis, abdominal pain, and chronic diarrhea have been reported (Borgono[~] et al., 1977; Majumdar et al., 2009; Guha Mazumder and Dasgupta, 2011). In rhesus macaques exposed to high doses of As(III) (7.5 mg/kg/da), which died within 28 days of the start of dosing, there were signs of acute inflammation and hemorrhage of the small intestine (Heywood and Sortwell, 1979). Prolonged exposure (104 weeks) of rodents to MMA(V)

(10e1000 mg/kg), one of the metabolites of inorganic As, showed that the large intestine is the target organ of this As species (Arnold et al., 2003). Toxicity of the large intestine occurred at concentrations well above levels to which humans are normally exposed. The no-effect level for intestinal toxicity was assessed as 50 mg/kg for rats and female mice and 200 mg/kg for male mice. In general, there was thickening of the GI wall, edemas, hemorrhages and necrosis, and ulcerations or perforations of the mucosa of the large intestine; and also a significant increase in the incidence of squamous metaplasia of absorptive epithelial cells of the colon and rectum. In vitro studies have clearly shown that inorganic As and its metabolites have a considerable effect on intestinal cells. Calatayud et al. (2014, 2015) showed that exposure to trivalent arsenicals generates a pro-inflammatory response (increase of the cytokines IL-6, IL-8, and TNFa), which is translated, in the case of DMA(III), into an increase in permeability of the epithelial monolayer.

Finally, there are effects on intestinal microbiota. Studies in rodents dosed with As(III) (10 mg/L) for 4 weeks showed alterations of the gut microbiome community at the abundance level and disturbance of metabolic profiles at the function level (Lu et al., 2014). This might also be a mechanism by which As exposure leads to GI disorders.

## 6. Conclusions

As has been commented in this review and shown in the various thematic areas that have been discussed, the influence of the gut environment is very important for the final toxicity exerted by these trace elements. Therefore, further progress in their understanding is crucial to characterize the mode of action of these toxic elements and to modulate their toxicity through even the dietary components themselves.
